extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of mathematical olympiads / competition combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt (problems and solutions) illustrating applications of the Box (Pigeonhole) Principle in combinatorics, number theory, and graph coloring (Ramsey theory). Contains worked examples (E8–E15), definitions (Ramsey numbers, sum-free sets, Schur function), bounds, constructions, and many exercise statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (box principle) — counting to force repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: If objects are placed into a limited number of 'boxes' (possibilities), then some box must contain at least two objects when the number of objects exceeds the number of boxes. Use counts of possible remainders/pairs/cells to force repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: count possible distinct pairs/remainders/positions (e.g., pairs of consecutive terms modulo m, remainders of powers modulo m, cells in a partition of a region). When number of items exceeds number of possible distinct states, some state repeats and that repetition yields the desired conclusion (periodicity, divisibility, overlap, etc.). Examples in the text include sequences modulo 10, powers modulo 10^n, geometric subdivisions, and residue classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity of linear recurrences modulo m via pairs of consecutive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two consecutive terms of a linear recurrence (e.g., Fibonacci) determine all succeeding and preceding terms; thus, working modulo m, the sequence is purely periodic once a pair repeats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form pairs (a_n, a_{n+1}) modulo m; there are only m^2 possible pairs, so by pigeonhole some pair repeats and the sequence cycles. In particular, the first repeating pair in the Fibonacci-type examples is (1,1). Applied in E8 and E9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit period bound for Fibonacci-type sequence modulo 10
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sequence defined by a_{n+1} = a_{n-1} + a_n with addition mod 10 (starting 1,1,...), the sequence is purely periodic and the period is at most 99.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: considering 101 successive terms gives 100 consecutive pairs; excluding the impossible pair (0,0) leaves only 99 distinct pairs mod 10, so two pairs repeat. Thus period ≤ 99. (E8)

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of Fibonacci number divisible by 10^n and period bound modulo 10^n
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n, the Fibonacci sequence modulo 10^n is periodic and contains 0; hence there is a Fibonacci number ending with n zeros. The period length is at most 10^{2n} − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take 10^{2n}+1 terms to form 10^{2n} pairs; the pair (0,0) cannot occur, so only 10^{2n} − 1 possible pairs exist and repetition implies a zero occurs. (E9)

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers modulo m produce residue 1 when base coprime to m (powers method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If gcd(a,10) = 1 (or more generally gcd(a,m)=1), then for any n there exists a power of a that is congruent to 1 modulo 10^n (i.e., ends with 000...01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the list a, a^2, ..., a^{10^n} mod 10^n: there are only 10^n − 1 nonzero residues, so two powers have the same remainder; their quotient is ≡1 (mod 10^n). Since gcd(a,10^n)=1 we can cancel the factor to get a^k ≡ 1 (mod 10^n). (E10)

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-covering pigeonhole technique (incremental coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: When placing multiple shapes of fixed area in a region of smaller total area, track how much new area each successive shape covers: if pairwise overlaps are assumed small, the sum of 'newly covered' areas exceeds the region's area, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in E11: placing nine rugs of area 1 in a room of area 5; assuming every pair overlaps by <1/9 leads to a lower bound for total covered area exceeding 5, contradiction; hence some pair overlap ≥ 1/9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-coloring/pigeonhole at a vertex to force monochromatic subgraph
rubrics_metrics.description: In an n-coloring of the complete graph G_p, choosing any vertex P, among the p−1 incident edges at least ceil((p−1)/n) have the same color; this can be used to force monochromatic small subgraphs (triangles, K_q) by repeated application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In G6 with 2 colors, from one vertex at least 3 incident edges share a color, leading to either a monochromatic triangle or a complementary monochromatic triangle; this yields R(3,3) ≤ 6 (E12). Similar logic used in multi-color cases (E13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Ramsey Numbers R(q1,...,qn)
rubrics_metrics.description: If q1,...,qn ≥ 2 are integers, there is a minimal number R(q1,...,qn) so that for any n-coloring of the complete graph with p ≥ R(q1,...,qn) vertices, for at least one i the graph contains a monochromatic complete subgraph on q_i vertices (a monochromatic G_{q_i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These R-values are the central objects of Ramsey theory; trivial cases include R(q,2)=q. The text lists known small values and uses Ramsey numbers to relate to sum-free partitions and Schur's function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction method for lower bounds via group partitions (avoid monochromatic triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can construct an n-coloring of a complete graph without monochromatic K_3 (triangle) by labeling vertices with elements of an abelian group and coloring edge xy by x+y, partitioning nonzero group elements into sum-free sets corresponding to colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E13 constructs a 3-coloring of G16 without monochromatic triangle using the elementary abelian group of order 16 and three sum-free subsets A1,A2,A3. This gives lower bounds on Ramsey numbers via explicit colorings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive upper bound and factorial-type estimate for Ramsey numbers R_n(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define p_n minimal p such that any n-coloring of K_p forces a monochromatic triangle. Then q_n = p_n − 1 satisfies q_{n+1} = (n+1) q_n + 1, leading to q_n < e · n! and hence p_n ≤ e · n! + 1, so R_n(3) ≤ e n! + 1 (E14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive recurrence from partitioning and counting; use truncated series for e to estimate q_n; yields explicit (crude) upper bounds for Ramsey numbers. The text uses this to get asymptotic upper bounds and numeric estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of known small Ramsey numbers / empirical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Known exact or computed Ramsey numbers cited: R(3,3)=6, R(3,3,3)=17, R(3,4)=9, R(4,4)=18, R(3,6)=18, R(3,5)=14, R(3,7)=23, R(4,5)=25 (the last found by large computation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific values are used to produce concrete combinatorial statements (e.g., existence of monochromatic triangles/tetrahedra in groups of given size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum-free sets and Schur function f(n) — definitions and bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset A of positive integers (or abelian group) is sum-free if x+y=z has no solution with x,y,z ∈ A. Schur's function f(n) is the largest integer such that {1,...,f(n)} can be partitioned into n sum-free subsets. Known values: f(1)=1, f(2)=4, f(3)=13, f(4)=44 (Baumert). Schur's estimates: (3n−1)/2 ≤ f(n) ≤ e n! − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and bounds are used to relate Ramsey numbers and sum-free partitions; the upper bound is derived by applying Ramsey's theorem to a graph constructed from the partition (see next rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting sum-free partition problems into colored graph problems (difference-coloring method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partition of {1,...,N} into n parts A_1,...,A_n, construct a complete graph on labeled vertices and color edge rs with color m if |r−s| ∈ A_m. A monochromatic triangle then corresponds to x,y,z ∈ A_m with x+y=z, contradicting sum-freeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show that any partition of {1,...,e n!} into n parts contains a non-sum-free part; thus f(n) ≤ e n! − 1. Also used to show R_n(3) ≥ f(n) + 2 by reversing the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative size/difference pigeonhole argument for proving impossibility of partitions (chain-of-differences method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a set {1,...,M} cannot be partitioned into n sum-free subsets, pick the largest part which must have at least ceil(M/n) elements; form differences with its largest element and place those differences into remaining parts; iterate this size-division procedure to force progressively smaller subsets until a contradiction (an impossible difference) arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in E15 to show {1,...,1957} cannot be partitioned into six sum-free subsets by the chain 327,66,17,6,3 leading to two differences whose further difference is outside all parts; this gives a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric subdivision pigeonhole: subdivide region into cells to force multiple points per cell
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a geometric region into a fixed grid or number of parts (e.g., subdivide unit square into 25 squares of side 1/5) so that a disk/cube/cell of prescribed size covers a whole cell. With sufficiently many points (or objects), some cell must contain the required number of points/coverage property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in problem solutions: (i) cover three insects by a disk radius 1/7 via 5×5 subdivision (problem 17); (ii) with 342 points in 7×7×7 cube, subdivide into 343 unit cubes to find an empty one (problem 18); (iii) subdivide circle circumference into arcs (problem 52).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue / remainder pigeonhole tricks for divisibility and digit-pattern problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider sequences of numbers (e.g., 1,11,111,...) or powers (a,a^2,...) modulo n (or 10^n). There are only finitely many remainders, so either a remainder 0 appears or two entries share the same remainder and their difference yields a multiple with the desired form (e.g., a number of only ones or a power ending with prescribed digits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in problems: existence of multiple of n consisting entirely of ones when n not divisible by 2 or 5 (problem 19); selecting subset with sum divisible by n via cumulative sums mod n (problem 20); E10 and related arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference / consecutive-differences counting for equal differences or repeated counts
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences of integers within bounds, consider consecutive differences (a_{i+1}−a_i). There are only so many possible distinct values, so repeated differences or pigeonhole on the sum can force several equal differences or other combinatorial conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in problem 15: among 20 distinct integers <70, pairwise differences contain four equal numbers; argument sums consecutive differences and bounds lead to contradiction if too few repeats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive inequality for Ramsey numbers R(r,s)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as problem 42 and used to derive binomial-type upper bounds for R(r,s) (problem 43). This recurrence is a standard tool to get explicit upper bounds via induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: General problem-solving heuristics illustrated (select extremal element, parity/mod arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common devices: pick an extremal element (largest, smallest, furthest), apply parity or modular arithmetic, partition into cases or cells, use extremal/iterative selection with pigeonhole at each stage to force structure or contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the chapter: choosing a vertex with many same-color edges (E12–E14), choosing the largest element of a subset and studying its differences (E15), partitioning intervals or grids (problems 17,18,52–56), and modular parity reasoning (problems 16,31,19). These are generic rubrics for approaching pigeonhole-style problems.
